item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Tue Oct 20 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Tue Oct 20 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Tue Oct 20 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers

item.title: CANCELED: Inclusive Movement & Body Positivity — Tue Oct 20, 5:30 PM — WILLIAM LEON GARRETT FIELDHOUSE
item.description:
Break down the barriers of gym intimidation in a welcoming, low-pressure environment. This workshop will explore body-positive movement, navigating recreation and fitness spaces with confidence, and approaches to gender-affirming fitness. Participants will be guided through a light, accessible yoga routine followed by conversation and Q&A with Katie Landrum. Come as you are all outfits, clothing, experience levels, and relationships with movement are welcome. No prior yoga or fitness experience is needed. Location: Bill Garrett Fieldhouse RSVP in advance—space is limited. All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.
Source: IU LGBTQ+ Culture Center

item.title: It's On Us: Bystander Intervention Workshop — Tue Oct 20, 6:00 PM — Global & International Studies Building
item.description:
The It’s On Us: Bystander Intervention Workshop is a 90-minute, audience-driven bystander intervention program that teaches students the skills needed to help in situations involving alcohol and drug use that could lead to a sexual assault. Students practice helping in real-life scenarios and discuss how alcohol and drug use influences a person’s ability to give and get consent to engage in sexual activity with another person.
It's On Us is required for all first-year and transfer undergraduate students. You must attend one session to fulfill the requirement.
Instructions:
Those who arrive more than 5 minutes after the start time will NOT be allowed into the session and will need to attend a different session
If this is your assigned workshop but you cannot attend it in its entirety, please RSVP for a different workshop.
If you have concerns about attending due to personal experiences or need to request accommodations, please contact the office at itsonus@iu.edu.
A

item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Sat Oct 24 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Sat Oct 24 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Sat Oct 24 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. item.title: Embedded Counseling (CAPS) — Mon Oct 26, 8:00 AM — LGBTQ+ CULTURE CENTER
item.description:
Supporting your well-being is an important part of our work at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center. That's why we are proud to partner with Counseling & Psychological Services (CAPS) to provide an embedded counselor in our space every Monday from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Mollibeth Penner, LHMCA serves as our embedded counselor and works directly with students connected to the LGBTQ+ Culture Center. To schedule an appointment, please call CAPS (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/make-appointment/index.html) and let them know you are an LGBTQ+ Culture Center student interested in meeting with Mollibeth at the center. We hope this partnership makes it easier for you to access support in a space where you feel comfortable and affirmed. All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.
Source: IU LGBTQ+ Culture Center

item.title: Home Away from Home: Student Life on Campus — Mon Oct 26, 9:00 AM — HERMAN B WELLS LIBRARY
item.description:
Spanning across four decades—1970s to the 2000s—items including scrapbooks, photographs, student papers, and handbooks demonstrate life on and off campus. From decorating dorm rooms to chasing campus ghosts, students have always found ways to build community and make new memories. This exhibit highlights the student experience and the multitude of ways students found a sense of home, identity and belonging at Indiana University.

item.description: The CRS Op-Ed Initiative, open to faculty, students, and the CRS community, teaches participants how to convert research insights into accessible, public-facing op-eds. This four-course series covers how to develop, write, edit, and publish op-eds, and why opinion writing is an important vessel for spreading innovative ideas and sparking important discussions. Participants do not need any prior publication experience to join, and the course is free.The series is led by Assistant Director Meredith Perkins, who has six years of experience writing over 50 op-eds as a freelance journalist in student, local, and national publications.
